chunks: "A rotary encoder is a sensor on the shaft that turns rotation into electrical signals.

The most common type is an incremental quadrature encoder: a disc with a pattern of slots or magnetic poles, read by two sensors offset by a quarter of a pitch, so I get two square waves, A and B, 90 degrees out of phase.
Each edge is a fixed small angle. Which channel leads tells me direction, and counting both edges of both channels gives four times the lines of the disc.
There's usually an index pulse once per revolution for homing. The other type is absolute, which outputs a unique code at each angle so it knows where it is at power-up.
For speed, there are two ways, same as any pulse train.
I can count edges over a fixed window, say one control period of a millisecond, and divide by the window and the counts per rev.
That's simple and smooth at high speed, but at low speed I only get a few counts per window and the speed estimate is quantised.
Or I can time the gap between edges with a hardware timer and take the reciprocal, which is precise at low speed but updates only when an edge arrives.
In a real servo I'd use the timer's hardware quadrature mode, so the MCU counts without the CPU, and combine both methods."
